papers.title: Objective sleep tracking for fatigue management in cargo pilots: six months of continuous smart-ring monitoring
papers.abstract: Aviation fatigue management estimates crew sleep from rosters and self-report. We examined how sleep duration changes around flights and with departure and landing times. In an observational cohort study, 13 cargo pilots wore an Ultrahuman smart ring for six months in 2026. We linked 1,504 sleep sessions to the flown schedule. Linear mixed-effects models compared each sleep session with the same pilot's rest nights, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Total sleep time was 48 min shorter on the night before a flight (95% CI 32 to 65 min) and 28 min shorter in the first sleep after one (95% CI 13 to 43 min). Later nights did not differ. Sleep duration varied with clock time. Compared with evening departures and landings, respectively, pilots slept 57 min less before a departure between 06:00h and 11:59h (95% CI 14 to 101 min) and 97 min less after a landing between 00:00h and 05:59h (95% CI 37 to 156 min). Flight direction and length showed no association. Differences between pilots explained 14.1% of the variance in total sleep time, more than six times the 2.2% explained by duty position. Fatigue risk management could plan rest around departure and landing times.

papers.title: "It Just Puts You Out!" Tranq Sleep, Sensory Discernment, and the Experience of Consuming Xylazine-Adulterated Fentanyl in Rural North Carolina
papers.abstract: Background: Xylazine, a veterinary sedative not approved for human use, has emerged as a consequential adulterant in the U.S. illicit fentanyl supply. Although a growing body of qualitative research has documented the experiences of fentanyl consumers exposed to tranq in large Northeastern cities, little is known about how xylazine is experienced in rural or Southern regions where the evolution of the illicit drug supply often lags behind its urban equivalents. This study examines how fentanyl consumers in west-central North Carolina detect, comprehend and respond to the widespread adulteration of fentanyl markets with xylazine. Methods: Between September and December of 2025, a seasoned interviewer conducted 25 in-depth, semi-structured qualitative interviews with fentanyl consumers recruited from both fixed and mobile syringe service programs in Gaston and Burke County, North Carolina. Interviews explored sensory discernment strategies, pharmacologic effects, and behavioral responses to the presence of xylazine. Data were analyzed using a combined deductive-inductive thematic approach in QSR NVivo 14.0. Results: Participants described a distinctive repertoire of sensory strategies for identifying xylazine in their fentanyl supply, including the appearance of drug residue on foil, bitterness and chemical odor when smoked, and altered viscosity when injected. A minority described an inability to detect xylazine through sensory cues. Participants consistently distinguished a profound involuntary sedation they called tranq sleep from the familiar opioid nod, characterizing it by nearly instantaneous loss of consciousness with severe withdrawal upon awakening. While nearly all participants expressed strong aversion to xylazine, a meaningful minority valued its amplifying effects to improve a diminishing fentanyl high. Conclusions: This study offers among the first qualitative description of xylazine exposure in a rural fentanyl market. Findings extend the xylazine literature geographically and pharmacologically and underscore the urgency of harm reduction responses tailored to the distinctive harms of xylazine. In particular, adverse health outcomes that accumulate during episodes of protracted and unarousable sedation, including physical injury, victimization, and the severe withdrawal syndrome that follows upon awakening.

papers.title: Enablers and barriers to scaling an ECD parenting program into primary health care services in rural Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Early childhood development programs play a crucial role in fostering child development. However, scaling-up these programs in low- and middle-income countries poses significant challenges. We conducted a mixed-method study of an evidence-based early childhood parenting program integrated into the primary health care services (community clinics) across four districts in rural Bangladesh. The program caters to caregivers of children aged 6-36 months with mild-to-moderate malnutrition. The parenting program is delivered by government community health workers (CHWs) with small groups of mother-child dyads within the community clinic setting as part of their routine duties. Mothers-child dyads attend fortnightly sessions for one year. CHWs are trained and monitored by government supervisors with overall oversight provided by government health staff at the sub-district and district level. The aim of the study was to identify the strengths and weaknesses of the program and strategies for improvement. Quantitative data included data from clinic logbooks, observations of session quality (n=60), and in-person interviews with participating mothers (n=185) in sixty clinics and phone interviews with mothers (n=164) in a further eighty clinics. Qualitative data included in-depth interviews with CHWs (n=20), government inspectors (n=16), and managers (n=4), and focus group discussions with mothers (n=4 groups, n=30 mothers), and grandmothers (n=4 groups, n=28 grandmothers) across twelve clinics. Results indicated that the key enablers to program implementation included strong government ownership, high compliance in implementing the program by CHWs, adequate session quality, satisfactory session attendance, and positive attitudes towards the program by all stakeholders. Key barriers included low levels of supervision, insufficient advocacy messaging within the community, poor communication across health staff at the different levels, and challenges in providing play materials at scale. The findings are being used to inform revisions to the program to enhance implementation fidelity and sustainability within the health system.

papers.title: Building a community-academic partnership in public housing: Lessons from applying the CBPR Partnership Readiness Model
papers.abstract: The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) eating plan has been shown to reduce hypertension; however, adherence is low among low-income African American (AA) women, who experience a disproportionate burden of hypertension. To better understand barriers to DASH among low-income AA women, specifically AA women living in public housing, we established a community-academic partnership using a project advisory board (PAB). This paper applies the CBPR Partnership Readiness Model to assess community stakeholder readiness for the partnership. PAB members were recruited through ongoing research and volunteer work in the target community. We developed a 33-page PAB workbook clarifying study goals, member roles and expectations, and hypertension information. A questionnaire was used to gather feedback on members' experiences. PAB membership increased by 150% after the first year following a second recruitment phase. Members reported satisfaction with progress toward local food equity initiatives and with partnership sustainability. Findings indicate the model was helpful in evaluating the PAB formation process for a project involving public housing stakeholders. PABs can help build local support for community-engaged projects. When members can see the advantages of their involvement, partnerships are strengthened.

papers.title: Physician-reported practices regarding obesity management in patients aged under 60 years with osteoarthritis in Jordan: a cross-sectional survey
papers.abstract: Obesity is an important modifiable risk factor for the development and progression of osteoarthritis (OA), particularly in weight-bearing joints. However, limited information is available regarding physicians practices in addressing obesity among patients with OA in Jordan. This study assessed self-reported obesity-management practices among physicians caring for patients aged under 60 years with OA. Methods We conducted an anonymous, cross-sectional convenience survey between December 2021 and January 2022. Physicians from orthopaedics, family medicine, general internal medicine, and rheumatology were recruited through professional networks and social-media platforms. Participants worked in Ministry of Health, private, university, and military healthcare institutions in Jordan. The questionnaire assessed obesity-related counselling, weight or body mass index (BMI) monitoring, consultation time, and referral for weight-reduction interventions among patients aged under 60 years with obesity and OA. Results A total of 308 physicians completed the questionnaire. Of these, 162 (52.6%) were orthopedic specialists or trainees and 146 (47.4%) were from other specialties, including primary care, general internal medicine, rheumatology, and general surgery. A total of 138 (44.8%) respondents worked in Ministry of Health healthcare institutions, 87 (28.2%) worked in the private sector, and 83 (26.9%) worked in university or military institutions. Eighty-five respondents (27.6%) reported explaining the effect of obesity on weight-bearing joints to almost all patients with obesity and OA, whereas 149 (48.4%) did so for approximately half of their patients and 74 (24.0%) rarely or never did so. Only 26 respondents (8.4%) reported monitoring weight or BMI in almost all target patients, while 187 (60.7%) reported doing so rarely or in only a few patients. Referral for dietetic or other weight-reduction interventions was reported for almost all target patients by 31 respondents (10.1%), whereas 152 (49.4%) reported rarely or never making such referrals. The remaining respondents reported counselling, monitoring, or referral for approximately half of their target patients. Conclusions Among participating physicians in Jordan, obesity counselling, weight or BMI monitoring, and referral for weight-reduction interventions were inconsistently incorporated into the management of patients aged under 60 years with OA. These findings support the integration of routine weight assessment, structured obesity counselling, and accessible multidisciplinary referral pathways into OA care. Because this study used convenience sampling and self-reported data, the findings should not be assumed to represent all physicians practising in Jordan.

papers.title: The toll of an early bell? School start time and adolescent sleep quality in Flanders, Belgium
papers.abstract: Study objectives: Adolescent sleep deprivation is a major public health concern, with insufficient and poor-quality sleep associated with adverse physical, mental and cognitive outcomes. Early school start times may contribute to sleep restriction by conflicting with the biologically delayed sleep patterns that emerge during puberty. This study examined the effect of school start times on sleep duration and sleep quality among secondary school students. Methods: Data were obtained from the 2022 Flemish Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study, including 12,329 adolescents from grade 1 to 6 in 94 secondary schools in Flanders. School start times were obtained from participating schools and sleep duration and sleep quality were assessed using self-report measures. Data were analyzed using traditional statistical methods (i.e., linear regression) and debiased machine learning methods (i.e., assumption lean regression, dose response curves and modified treatment policies). Results: No clinically meaningful effects of school start times on sleep outcomes were observed. In machine learning models, a 10-minute delay in start time was associated with non-significant changes in sleep quality (0.01 points on a 1-5 scale; 95% CI, -0.05 to 0.06) and school-day sleep duration (3.5 minutes; 95% CI, -1.0 to 8.0). Conclusions: Within the narrow range of school start times observed in Flemish secondary schools, confidence intervals excluded clinically meaningful effects of later start times on adolescent sleep duration and sleep quality. Whether larger delays would improve sleep remains to be determined.

papers.title: Risk Omission and Limited Disclosure in Dietary Supplement Promotion by Social Media Influencers
papers.abstract: Importance: Dietary supplements carry risks including adverse effects, drug interactions, and contamination-related harms, yet are frequently marketed without premarket requirements for efficacy or safety. Social media influencers have become a primary source through which people encounter and make decisions about supplements, but whether they communicate clinically relevant risks alongside claimed benefits remains unclear. Objective: To investigate how dietary supplements are presented by Instagram influencers, focusing on supplement types, advertising disclosure, persuasive strategies, and communication of benefits and harms. Design, Setting, and Participants: Cross-sectional content analysis of 1,120 dietary supplement presentations in 727 Instagram posts by 84 influencer accounts identified through audience-centered purposive sampling from two independent youth-focused studies in Switzerland and Austria. Main Outcomes and Measures: Main outcomes were supplement types, overall tone, advertising disclosure, persuasive strategies, and communication of benefits and harms, all summarized descriptively. Logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors assessed whether influencer type or supplement category influenced presentation characteristics. Results: Of 1,120 supplement presentations, 1092 (97.5%) were promotional in tone, 1088 (97.1%) involved advertising, but disclosure was absent in 802 advertisements (73.7%). Protein (463 [41.3%]), caffeine (156 [13.9%]), creatine (71 [6.3%]), and (multi-)vitamins (67 [6.0%]) were the most frequently identified ingredients. Benefits were mentioned in 269 presentations (24.0%); harms in only 26 (2.3%), mostly framing supplements as unnecessary or cautioning about side effects. No presentation mentioned drug interactions, contamination risks, or contraindications. Benefit claims were more common in presentations featuring micronutrient and miscellaneous ingredient supplements, and less common in presentations featuring sport nutrition supplements. Influencers with health credentials were more likely to include evidence cues than nonprofessionals (adjusted OR, 81.05; 95% CI, 13.76-477.44); associations with tone and personal experience narratives were not robust to adjustment. Conclusions and Relevance: Influencer presentation of supplements was highly commercialized, largely undisclosed, and characterized by a substantial imbalance between benefit and risk communication. The absence of clinically relevant risk information suggests that individuals relying on such content are unlikely to receive balanced safety information, underscoring the need for stronger regulation and proactive clinician inquiry about supplement use.

papers.title: A statistical calibration framework for subnational health surveillance from routine data and survey audits
papers.abstract: In many low- and middle-income countries, where civil registration and vital statistics remain incomplete, decision makers rely on estimates derived from large international household surveys. Those surveys are rarely powered for frequent subnational estimates, and the contraction in international aid has made their future uncertain. Small area estimation has supplemented them with increasingly available routine health records and satellite imagery to improve their precision, but the survey estimate remains the response variable. We propose a statistical calibration framework that inverts the roles of the two data sources, whereby the routine records provide a biased baseline estimator continuously over time at the subnational level of interest, while a probability survey is used intermittently to audit and adjust for the selection bias of the direct register estimator. We develop the corresponding modelling and estimation methods, including diagnostic and analysis tools for the transport assumption that the out-of-survey subpopulations and time points require. The proposed framework is applied in four African countries to estimate undiagnosed HIV positivity by district and the selection bias by age and sex, and we explain how it applies to other health surveillance needs with similar data settings.

papers.title: Toward Standards for Responsible AI in Health Communication: A Dual Method Pre-Deployment Risk Evaluation Framework and Case Study
papers.abstract: Context: Generative AI tools are increasingly being considered for use in public health research and practice, yet standardized frameworks for pre-deployment evaluation of the risks AI tools pose - across dimensions of platform safety, audience appropriateness, and user readiness - have not been established for health communication contexts. Program or Policy: We developed and implemented a dual-method pre-deployment evaluation framework that combines adversarial red-teaming and structured user testing to assess the readiness of a health communication AI tool. The framework was applied to the Trusted Health Information Assistant (THIA), a retrieval-augmented generation chatbot designed by NORC at the University of Chicago for use in public health communication research. Implementation: The framework was implemented sequentially, beginning with red-teaming to identify safety, audience appropriateness, and reliability concerns before engaging end users. Five independent testers completed 28 structured red-team prompts, after which identified issues were remediated and verified. User testing was subsequently conducted with six participants (e.g., caregivers of older adults) and included direct interaction with THIA, pre- and post-survey assessments, semi-structured interviews, and a review of backend analytics. Evaluation: The sequential, dual-method design successfully identified distinct categories of risk. Red-teaming identified platform integrity issues, including personally identifiable information (PII) handling and citation reliability. User testing subsequently assessed platform readiness under real-world conditions, surfacing trust dynamics and usability patterns. The convergence of findings across both methods validated the complementary design: each method identified distinct dimensions, together producing a more thorough and actionable assessment. Discussion: As generative AI tools increasingly enter public health research and practice, ensuring that potential risks are systematically identified and addressed before they reach end users is paramount. Yet the field lacks shared standards for pre-deployment evaluation. AI developers rarely publish evaluation findings, leaving public health organizations with few replicable models to guide their own assessments. This report addresses that gap by documenting a structured, sequential framework including methods, instruments, scoring rubrics, and reporting structures for evaluating health communication AI tools prior to deployment.

papers.title: Hand sanitizer recalls during the COVID-19 pandemic: a descriptive analysis of regulatory records from Canada, Nepal, Singapore and the USA
papers.abstract: Background: Alcohol-based hand sanitizers were central to infection prevention during the COVID-19 pandemic. The abrupt rise in global demand fueled the emergence of substandard and unregulated products. Government regulatory bodies around the globe responded to this issue by tightening quality control and enforcing stringent limits on contaminants. This study aimed to descriptively analyze the reasons for, and timing of hand sanitizer recalls and safety warnings between 2020 and 2024. Methodology: We extracted publicly available records from the national regulators of Canada, Nepal, Singapore, and the USA. The database was analyzed by country, year, and reason for recall to identify the recall patterns and regulatory practices. Results: We identified 1044 recalled products in Canada (277), Nepal (39), Singapore (26), and the USA (702). Major reasons for recall were administrative reasons such as non-compliance, nonresponse to the regulator, and unregistered or unauthorized sale (43.9%) followed by contamination with hazardous chemicals such as methanol, acetaldehyde, and benzene (37.4%) and subpotent ethanol or isopropanol (15.6%). Two-thirds of the recall records were from the USA followed by Canada, Nepal, and Singapore. While most of the recalls were announced during the first year of COVID-19, the recalls did not follow a temporal trend. Conclusion: The recall records showcased product hazard risks during the pandemic, highlighting its global impacts. The recalls in each of the four countries may have missed other substandard hand sanitizer products. This underlines the importance of strict monitoring and public awareness for product safety. The recall records discussed in this paper describe regulatory activity and should not be read as the prevalence of substandard hand sanitizers. Robust emergency regulatory frameworks, rapid analytical verification, and distributed yet strictly monitored certified production systems may help reduce public health risks due to hand sanitizers in the future.

papers.title: Laboratory evaluation of five rapid diagnostic tests for the serological diagnosis of chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection in Yucatan, Mexico
papers.abstract: Chagas disease (CD), caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, is a significant public health challenge in Latin America, where an estimated 70% of infected individuals remain undiagnosed. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) offer a promising solution for new screening strategies, yet their performance has not been systematically assessed in Mexican cohorts. Here, we evaluated the diagnostic performance of five RDTs: Chagas Rapid Test (Certum), Bio-Chagas Rapid Test (Mexlab), BiolineTM Chagas Ab (Abbott), Chagas Rapid Test (Amunet) and Chagas Sero K-SeT (Coris BioConcept). Performance was tested using 79 archived human serum samples from Yucatan. All tests were benchmarked against the diagnostic reference algorithm established by the Mexican Official Norm (NOM), where samples were characterised as positive if they were reactive to [≥] 2 conventional serological assays (Chagatest Lisado, Chagatest Recombinante v4.0 and Chagatest HAI). The RDTs demonstrated variable diagnostic sensitivity. The BiolineTM Chagas Ab test demonstrated the highest sensitivity (97.2%, 95% CI: 85.5 - 99.9; 35/36 positive samples detected) and almost perfect statistical agreement with the NOM reference algorithm ({kappa}= 0.90; p < 0.0001). Similarly, the Chagas Sero K-SeT prototype showed a high sensitivity (91.7%, 95% CI: 77.5 - 98.2; 33/36 positive samples detected) and substantial concordance ({kappa}= 0.87, p < 0.0001) with the NOM-based composite result. In contrast, the remaining RDTs demonstrated low sensitivities (Certum: 0.0%, 95% CI: 0.0-9.7; Mexlab: 5.6%, 95% CI: 0.7-18.7; Amunet: 33.3%, 95% CI: 18.6-51.0), limiting their suitability for CD diagnostic algorithms, at least in Yucatan. Specificity was consistently high across the RDTs, ranging from 93.0% to 100% (95% CIs: 80.9-100). These findings underscore the need to locally validate diagnostic tools. The BiolineTM Chagas Ab and Chagas Sero K-SeT tests met the WHO benchmarks for RDT performance and, if validated in larger cohorts, could strengthen the screening of T. cruzi infection and epidemiological surveillance in Mexico.

papers.title: Household cooking fuels, symptoms compatible with pneumonia and inequalities in care seeking among children under five in the Republic of the Congo: a nationally representative survey analysis
papers.abstract: Objectives: To examine the association between household cooking fuels and symptoms compatible with pneumonia, and socioeconomic inequalities in care seeking, among children under five in the Republic of the Congo. Methods: Secondary analysis of the 2014-2015 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey, the most recent national survey with available microdata on respiratory symptoms (9,159 children aged 0-59 months), using survey-weighted logistic regression. Results: The weighted prevalence of caretaker-reported cough with fast or difficult breathing due to a chest problem was 5.9% (95% CI 5.3-6.6). Compared with electricity or gas, cooking with solid fuels (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.23, 1.34-3.73) or kerosene (aOR 2.63, 1.38-5.01) was associated with higher odds of symptoms, independently of wealth, education and residence (E-values 3.9 and 4.7). Only 28.2% (23.1-33.9) of children with symptoms were taken to a health facility or provider, from 17.8% in the poorest to 61.1% in the richest quintile (aOR 4.10, 1.96-8.57 for the three richest versus the two poorest quintiles). Conclusions: Poorer Congolese children combine greater exposure to polluting cooking fuels and less access to care. Clean cooking policies should be combined with removal of financial barriers to care for sick children.

papers.title: Formative Evaluation to Inform Recruitment and Engagement Strategies for emergency activation of blood donors in Nimba County, Liberia
papers.abstract: While donations from voluntary non-remunerated donors are preferred, approximately 14% of blood donations globally come from family replacement and paid donors. In low- and middle-income countries, the proportion is higher, averaging 36.6% in low-income countries. However, much less is known about family replacement and paid donors relative to voluntary non-remunerated blood donors. It is known that family replacement and paid donors are often activated in response to an emergency in areas where blood is scarce and whole blood is the standard for transfusion. Thus, they are part of de facto civilian walking blood banks. Interest in civilian walking blood banks is increasing, but many operational best practices have not been established. The objective of this study was to better understand the motivations and donation experiences of family replacement and paid donors, as well as their attitudes toward possible donor-facing walking blood bank practices. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in Nimba County, Liberia, in May 2026 with participants who had donated blood in the last twelve months. Recruitment was conducted through radio announcements and snowball sampling. Transcripts were analyzed via directed content analysis using the Exploration, Preparation, Implementation, and Sustainment framework. Twelve donors, 11 men and one woman, participated. Many reported making donations both as family replacement and as paid donors. Participants reported altruism, positive past donation experiences, and a desire to help their families as donation facilitators. They reported distance, concern about pre-transfusion testing, and expenses incurred as donors as barriers. While they reported widespread concern about the effects of blood donation on the donor's health as a barrier to establishing a more formal walking blood bank approach, they typically believed outreach at community institutions would be an effective way to recruit new donors. These findings suggest that continued engagement among established donors in addition to recruitment of new donors is likely to increase the blood supply, although implementation questions around the best approaches to donor compensation and ensuring potential donors are paired with the closest facility remain.

papers.title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding priority zoonotic diseases (Mpox, Ebola, and Rabies) and associated factors among households in Bukavu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, 2025
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Zoonotic diseases are a major public health concern in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where diseases such as rabies, Ebola, and Mpox pose ongoing health risks. Household knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) play an important role in preventing zoonotic disease transmission. This study assessed household knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding priority zoonotic diseases in Bukavu, South Kivu Province, DRC, and identified factors associated with satisfactory overall KAP. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted from September 1 to 15, 2025, in the Bagira and Kadutu health zones of Bukavu. A total of 634 households were selected using two-stage cluster sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire administered through KoboCollect and analyzed using Stata version 17. The questionnaire assessed knowledge, attitudes, and practices concerning Ebola, Mpox, and rabies. Knowledge was measured using 17 items, attitudes using five-point Likert-scale items, and practices using five behavioral items. Scores of at least 70% were classified as satisfactory. Descriptive statistics, group comparisons, and bivariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used. Nonparametric tests were used when appropriate. Associations were reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Results: Overall, 42.9% of households demonstrated satisfactory knowledge of zoonotic diseases, 63.6% had favorable attitudes, and 11.7% demonstrated adequate preventive practices. Mpox was recognized as a zoonosis by 78.2% of respondents, Ebola by 66.6%, and rabies by 39.1%. Knowledge scores were higher among livestock-farming than non-livestock-farming households (p = 0.002). In the multivariable analysis of overall KAP, university-level education (OR = 12.06; 95% CI: 1.54-94.18; p = 0.018) and access to drinking water (OR = 6.74; 95% CI: 3.91-11.60; p < 0.001) were positively associated with satisfactory overall KAP. Conclusions: Households in Bukavu reported generally favorable attitudes toward zoonotic disease prevention, but satisfactory knowledge was less widespread and adequate preventive practices were uncommon. Interventions should help translate awareness and favorable attitudes into practical preventive behaviors through targeted risk communication and health education, alongside improvements in access to drinking water and sanitation. A coordinated One Health approach involving human, animal, and environmental health stakeholders may strengthen household-level prevention of priority zoonotic diseases. The findings can help inform locally tailored prevention strategies and identify priorities for future community-based research. Keywords: Zoonoses; Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices; One Health; Bukavu; Democratic Republic of the Congo

papers.title: Neuroimaging Inequities in Africa: Health system readiness, diagnostic capacity, and an embedded case study of portable ultra-low-field MRI implementation in Ethiopia
papers.abstract: Neurological conditions in Africa are an increasingly significant public health burden. Conditions such as stroke, dementia, and central nervous system infections impose a disproportionate burden in resource-constrained regions, highlighting the need to strengthen diagnostic capacity. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) are essential technologies for the diagnosis and management of these conditions. However, the availability and affordability of these advanced diagnostic technologies remain limited across the continent. A low-cost, portable ULF-MRI system may help expand access to neuroimaging services across diverse settings by overcoming some of the infrastructural and affordability challenges. The aim of this study was to assess the diagnostic imaging capacity and health system readiness for advanced neurological services in Africa and to examine the feasibility of integrating portable ULF-MRI into routine clinical care in a low-resource setting, specifically in Ethiopia. Quantitative data on MRI and CT capacity and selected health system infrastructure indicators were obtained from the World Health Organization Global Health Observatory Database. The qualitative case study was based on a recently deployed 0.064T ULF-MRI Hyperfine Swoop system at a regional specialized hospital in Ethiopia for clinical use. The results showed substantial gaps in diagnostic imaging capacity, workforce availability, and supporting infrastructure across Africa. MRI and CT density in Africa stood at 0.11 MRI and 0.42 CT scanners per million population, respectively. The Ethiopian case study suggested that ULF-MRI may be a promising approach to expanding neuroimaging access because it can be integrated into routine clinical practice with relatively modest infrastructure and personnel requirements. These findings underscore major diagnostic inequities across African health systems and suggest that portable ULF-MRI may offer a feasible approach to expanding access to neuroimaging services in resource-constrained settings. Key words: ultra-low field MRI, neuroimaging, global health equity, Africa, LMICs

papers.title: Sporadic detection of dengue virus RNA in California wastewater solids
papers.abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) is the most prevalent mosquito-borne virus globally, endemic in over 100 countries and associated with around 40,000 deaths each year. Prior research has shown that DENV RNA can be detected in wastewater, but detection rates vary widely depending on the setting and method used. In this study, we analyzed 1,072 untreated wastewater samples from five treatment plants in California, collected between December 2023 and December 2025, to evaluate wastewater-based surveillance for DENV. We compared wastewater data with reported clinical incidence and Aedes aegypti mosquito abundance measurements over the same period collected by the California Department of Public Health. DENV RNA was found in 1.2% of wastewater samples (13/1,072). DENV-1 was most common (0.6%, 6/1,072), followed by DENV-2 (0.4%, 4/1,072), and DENV-4 (0.3%, 3/1,072). No DENV-3 RNA was detected. DENV RNA was detected only in wastewater from southern California (plants in Los Angeles and San Diego counties), with no detections in wastewater from the Bay Area, including plants located in San Jose and Oakland. There was no correlation between wastewater DENV RNA levels and county-wide reported dengue incidence during the same week. However, counties with a higher incidence over the study period showed greater detection frequency of DENV RNA in wastewater. Weekly Ae. aegypti abundance was correlated with weekly incidence of locally-transmitted cases (Spearman's {rho}=0.45, p<0.01). Our results indicate that wastewater surveillance can detect DENV in areas of higher incidence, but the low detection frequency and sporadic nature of positive samples limit its utility as a standalone surveillance approach. Given the low incidence of dengue in California and the presence of robust clinical and mosquito surveillance systems, wastewater monitoring does not currently add significant public health value for dengue surveillance in the state.

papers.title: Cancer incidence in first-generation migrants and host populations in seven European registries, including Ukrainian-born migrants in Poland: a population-based study
papers.abstract: Background: Where people are born shapes their cancer risk, yet European cancer surveillance rarely records migration background. We estimated cancer incidence in first-generation migrants and assessed whether birth-country incidence stratifies their cancer risk. Methods: We harmonised data from six population-based cancer registries in Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain (Murcia, Tarragona), Italy (Turin), and Switzerland (Ticino) for 2003 to 2017, examining breast, colorectal, cervical, stomach, liver, and lung cancer in first-generation migrants and host populations. Countries of birth were grouped into quartiles of GLOBOCAN age-standardised incidence by cancer site and sex (birth-country incidence categories). We estimated cumulative risks (CR) and migrant-to-host cumulative risk ratios (CRR). Ukrainian-born migrants in Poland were analysed separately for 2022 and 2023. Findings: The cancer risk among individuals with a migration background increased with birth-country incidence for cervical, stomach, and liver cancer. For cervical cancer, CRR rose from close to 1 in migrants from low-incidence countries to 4,9 (95% CI 3,5-6,9) in those from high-incidence countries in Turin. Breast and colorectal cancer diagnosis risk was lower than in host populations in every category. Across the six cancers combined, migrants had lower risk in 9 of 11 registry and sex strata, as lower breast, colorectal, and lung cancer risk outweighed higher cervical, stomach, and liver cancer risk. Ukrainian-born migrants in Poland (n=4450) had higher CR at most anatomical sites than the host population. Interpretation: The cancer risk among individuals with a migration background relative to host populations depends on country of birth and cancer site. Birth-country incidence is a useful way of grouping migrants by risk. National averages can mask residual risk in subgroups, e.g. migrants born in high-incidence countries had up to five times the cervical cancer risk of host populations with rates near or below the WHO elimination threshold. Routine recording of country of birth can support risk-tailored prevention and cancer service planning for displaced populations.

papers.title: From non-uptake during early adolescence to acceptance during a catch-up campaign: a qualitative study of changing HPV vaccination decisions across two life stages among young women in Amsterdam, the Netherlands
authors: M. F. Schim van der Loeff
papers.abstract: BackgroundHuman Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination effectively prevents HPV-related disease, but its population-level impact depends on sufficient coverage. In 2023-2024, the Netherlands offered free HPV vaccination to individuals aged 19-27 years through a national catch-up campaign. For women, this was a second opportunity, as they had been offered vaccination at ages 9-13 through the National Immunisation Programme (NIP). Back then, uptake was relatively low (46-57% in these birth cohorts), but uptake increased to 55-63% following the catch-up vaccination. This campaign provided an apt opportunity to explore the factors underlying previous and current HPV vaccination decisions among the same women across two life stages. MethodsBetween May 2023 and May 2024, 16 semi-structured interviews were conducted in Amsterdam with women who accepted HPV vaccination during the catch-up after non-uptake during early adolescence. Interviews explored factors influencing non-uptake and later acceptance, guided by the Health Belief Model and additional sociocultural constructs. Data were analysed using thematic analysis with open and theory-guided coding in MAXQDA. ResultsNon-uptake during early adolescence was primarily shaped by parental decision-making, cultural and religious norms, fear of side effects, low perceived susceptibility to HPV and limited self-efficacy. Acceptance in young adulthood was driven by greater autonomy, higher perceived susceptibility, increased trust in accumulated vaccine evidence and accessible vaccination infrastructure. Peer influence replaced parental influence as the dominant social factor. ConclusionHPV vaccine decision-making is a dynamic process rather than fixed. Permanent catch-up HPV vaccination opportunities would enable young adults to make autonomous vaccination decisions as their circumstances change. Highlights- Adolescent HPV non-uptake was driven by parents, culture and safety fears; - Adult acceptance was driven by perceived risk, greater trust and peer influence; - Decision-making is a dynamic state, not a fixed one-time decision; - Free, accessible infrastructures to vaccination enabled catch-up uptake; - Catch-up HPV vaccination enables autonomous vaccine decisions in young adults.

papers.title: Association between Blood Lead Levels and Anaemia in a Pregnant Population in the Kintampo Area of Ghana: A Prospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundMaternal anaemia and lead exposure both pose substantial risks in pregnancy, but their relationship has not been consistently explored. We assessed trimester-specific blood lead levels (BLLs) and their association with anaemia in pregnant women in the Kintampo area of Ghana. MethodsIn this prospective cohort study nested within the PRISMA Maternal and Newborn Health Study in Ghana, 300 pregnant women were enrolled at <14 weeks gestation and followed until delivery. Trimester-specific venous blood was collected and analysed for haemoglobin levels using Sysmex XN 330 auto analyser (Sysmex Corporation, Japan) and BLL using inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Anaemia was defined as 11.0g/dL for first (T1) and third (T3) trimesters and 10.5g/dL for second (T2) trimester according to the World Health Organisations (WHOs) trimester-specific haemoglobin thresholds and elevated BLL as [≥]3.5 {micro}g/dL by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Multiple logistic regression, adjusted for maternal age, parity, education, malaria parasitaemia, body mass index, gestational age and occupation, examined the BLL and anaemia association. A population-averaged Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) model was used to assess the association between elevated BLL and anaemia across trimesters. ResultsThe mean age of participants was 27.7{+/-}5.8 years (range 18-44years). Geometric mean BLL increased significantly across trimesters from 1.0 to 1.3 to 1.5 {micro}g/dL (p=0.003) for T1, T2 and T3 respectively. The prevalence of elevated BLL ([≥]3.5 {micro}g/dL) was 10.7%, 7.6%, and 15.2% for T1, T2, and T3 respectively. Anaemia prevalence increased significantly with increasing trimester from 34.7.0% to 59.3% to 76.0% (p<0.001) for T1, T2 and T3 respectively. In the population-averaged GEE model, elevated BLL was associated with increased odds of anaemia across trimesters, though this did not reach statistical significance (OR = 1.29, 95% CI: 0.77-2.17, p = 0.327). ConclusionAnaemia prevalence in pregnancy is high in the Kintampo area and increases with advancing gestation. No significant association was observed between BLL and anaemia. These findings reinforce anaemia as a priority for urgent interventions in pregnancy through pathways independent of lead exposure. However, occupational lead surveillance and control remain important policy considerations.

papers.title: A lifecourse perspective on sociodemographic intersectional inequalities in physical and mental health outcomes
papers.abstract: Persistent inequalities in health outcomes continue to be a stubborn feature of many developed Western societies. To effectively understand health inequalities researchers must address two key criticisms: an overt focus on singular dimensions of disadvantage and a continuing need for longitudinal studies. Lifecourse intersectionality offers a framework to address these critiques through situating more nuanced and multidimensional understandings of the development of inequalities over time. We conduct a longitudinal Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) examining both physical and mental health SF12 scores using UK Household Longitudinal Study data for adults (2009 to 2023). Forming intersections based on sex, ethnicity, generational cohort, education, and socioeconomic class, we identify a substantial degree of intersectional variation in our outcomes, and distinct differences in the development of intersectional inequalities in physical and mental health over the lifecourse. Intersectional inequalities are more pronounced for mental health compared to physical health, particularly at younger and older ages. In both cases, inequalities are additively patterned with generation and sex appearing most important to mental health and socioeconomic differences being stronger for physical health. However, our results also emphasise heterogeneity in the identified lifecourse intersectional effects, particularly in relation to how the patterning of the sociodemographic components for mental health vary by generational cohort. We therefore help reveal important complexity in the development of health inequalities in the UK and highlight the utility of longitudinal intersectional MAIHDA as a tool for quantitative intersectional researchers.

papers.title: Characterizing the relative strength of metapopulation dynamics in measles persistence
papers.abstract: Background/AimsMeasles is a highly infectious, vaccine-preventable disease that remains persistent across much of the world despite continued large-scale control efforts. Local dynamics of measles are shaped by births of susceptible individuals and seasonal drivers of transmission, while broader regional dynamics are shaped by population mobility and metapopulation connectivity. Incidence data, useful for tracking the progress of measles control, are frequently reported only at the aggregate level (e.g., states/provinces), and persistence at this scale may arise because of the independent persistence in all local sub-units or because of regional metapopulation dynamics. Disentangling the contribution of local versus regional persistence is critical in identifying effective strategies for control. Methods/ResultsWe show, as vaccination reduces local measles prevalence, metapopulation colonization and extinction events dominate regional persistence. This manifests as a change in the seasonal distribution of cases throughout the year; incidence becomes more uniformly distributed through the year even with no change in underlying seasonal drivers. We demonstrate this using: 1) a seasonally forced, stochastic metapopulation compartmental model; 2) historical measles incidence in the USA; and 3) recent subnational-level measles incidence in Nigeria. We create a novel, scale-free measure to quantify the contribution of metapopulation dynamics to persistence, roundness, defined as the geometric mean of the scaled maximum and minimum monthly incidence. A low value of roundness indicates strong local persistence dominated by the seasonal attractor, while a high value indicates strong metapopulation persistence. We illustrate the properties of this measure using simulations and observed data. In the USA, roundness nearly doubled after the introduction of the measles-containing vaccine. In Nigeria, roundness is well correlated with observed vaccine coverage, with a Pearsons r of 0.70 (95% CI: 0.57, 0.80), discriminating between northern states dominated by local persistence of measles and southern states where persistence is maintained by regional dynamics. ConclusionIdentifying how measles persists is important in its control--vaccination strategies may differ if persistence is largely local, or if persistence is driven by connectivity from surrounding areas, even where yearly incidence is comparable. Our approach can be valuable areas where other measures (connectivity, mobility, laboratory confirmed illness) are not widely available.

papers.title: Risk-Factors of Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever Across Six Tertiary Hospitals in Afghanistan from 2022 to 2025: Reported Exposures, Healthcare-Worker Clustering, and Ribavirin Treatment-Timing Analyses
papers.abstract: IntroductionCrimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is endemic in Afghanistan, but multi-hospital data characterising reported exposure patterns, healthcare-worker clustering, and ribavirin-mortality associations after accounting for treatment timing are lacking. MethodsA retrospective cohort study included 737 laboratory-confirmed CCHF patients admitted to six tertiary hospitals in Afghanistan between January 2022 and December 2025. Reported exposures were assessed by occupation and tick-contact history. Clustering of healthcare-worker (HCW) infections during high caseload was assessed by permutation testing. Ribavirin-mortality association was assessed using multivariable Cox regression adjusted for clinical severity, age, sex, hospital, and comorbidity, with sensitivity analyses addressing treatment timing immortal-time bias. ResultsAmong 737 patients, the median age was 35 years and 78.3% were male. The hospitalization fatality ratio (HFR) was 27.7% (204/737). Of 574 patients with recorded occupation: 33.6% were livestock handlers, 12.9% slaughterhouse workers or butchers, 24.9% household meat preparers, and only 11.1% reported tick exposure. Nineteen patients were HCWs, and 18 became infected during periods of concurrent CCHF admissions, and clustering exceeded chance (p=0.012), consistent with healthcare-associated exposure during surges. Personal protective equipment (PPE) was used in 728 (98.6%) admissions, but its composition was incomplete: 532 (72.2%) comprised mask and gloves without a gown, and only 205 (27.8%) with mask, gloves, and gown. Isolation rooms were available for only 274 of 737 admissions (37.2%). Among 727 patients in the ribavirin analysis, 85.0% received treatment. Conventional analysis suggested lower mortality (adjusted HR 0.57) but affected by immortal-time bias. The association weakened for same-day treatment versus no treatment (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.41-0.96; sensitive to model specification) and was absent in time-varying analysis (HR 0.93). ConclusionCCHF in this hospitalised Afghan cohort was commonly associated with reported animal and livestock-related exposure, while healthcare-worker infections clustered during outbreak surges. Isolation capacity and caseload may be important correlates of healthcare-associated risk alongside PPE availability. Ribavirin findings were sensitive to treatment-timing adjustment and cannot establish a causal survival benefit. Key QuestionsO_LIWhat is already known on this topic O_LICCHF is endemic in Afghanistan, but previous studies lacked individual-level multi-hospital data on reported transmission exposures, formal assessment of healthcare-worker clustering, and ribavirin treatment-timing analyses, while evidence from other endemic countries has been inconsistent. C_LI C_LIO_LIWhat this study adds O_LIIn 737 laboratory-confirmed cases across six tertiary hospitals, reported animal and livestock-related exposure was far more common than reported tick exposure, healthcare-worker infections clustered significantly during periods of high CCHF caseload and where isolation capacity was limited, and the apparent mortality benefit of ribavirin was substantially attenuated after accounting for treatment timing and immortal-time bias. C_LI C_LIO_LIHow this study might affect research, practice or policy O_LIThe findings support stronger public health interventions such as One Health prevention at the animal-human interface, investment in dedicated isolation capacity together with complete PPE during outbreak surges, protective equipment during slaughter and butchering, veterinary surveillance of viraemic livestock, and risk-reduction before Eid-al-Adha. C_LI C_LI

papers.title: Evidence-Based WASHmobile Anticipatory Action Framework to Reduce Cholera Outbreaks during Extreme Weather Events in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
papers.abstract: Extreme weather contributes to cholera outbreaks globally. We examined associations between extreme weather and cholera through 4 years of surveillance at 115 healthcare facilities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and built an anticipatory action framework through WASHmobile for water, sanitation, and hygiene mobile messaging during extreme weather. Drought and wet conditions were defined using 3-month Standardized Precipitation Indices with CHIRPS data. A test-negative design assessed associations between extreme weather and culture-confirmed Vibrio cholerae among 1,068 diarrhea patients. Odds of cholera were higher during drought (OR: 1.94, 95% CI: 1.17-3.20) and extreme wet conditions (OR: 2.22, 95% CI: 1.39-3.55). During drought conditions in our randomized controlled trial of 2334 participants, handwashing with soap significantly declined in the standard arm but not the WASHmobile arm. Findings informed an anticipatory action framework where pre-defined climate triggers activate WASHmobile as an early warning system to reduce cholera outbreaks during extreme weather.

papers.title: Reporting Quality of Mendelian Randomization Studies Based on STROBE-MR: An Investigation Powered by Large Language Models
papers.abstract: 2BackgroundMendelian randomization (MR) has been widely used to investigate causal relationships between exposures and outcomes. However, concerns have also been raised about the reporting quality of MR studies. STROBE-MR was developed as a reporting guideline for MR studies, but assessments of compliance with STROBE-MR in published MR studies remain limited and rely largely on manual review. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), it is now possible to automate STROBE-MR compliance assessment. MethodsWe developed a pipeline using OpenAIs GPT-5-mini model for automated assessment of MR reporting quality. Model performance was evaluated on an annotated dataset of 46 eligible MR articles. We applied the pipeline to more than 13,000 MR articles published between 2005 and 2025 to assess compliance with the STROBE-MR guideline and to explore reporting patterns across STROBE-MR items, sections, and time periods. Complete compliance required reporting all applicable components of an item; a sensitivity analysis used a partial compliance criterion requiring at least one applicable component. ResultsOur LLM-based pipeline agreed with the human consensus on 89.0% of the STROBE-MR assessments. On average, 22 of 43 items (51.2%) met the complete compliance criterion, with substantial variation in reporting rates across STROBE-MR items and sections. The least reported items were found in the "Methods", "Results", and "Other Information" sections. The number of reported items remained stable over time, with slight decreases after 2021. Sensitivity analysis showed that temporal trend patterns differed between complete and partial compliance, particularly in the Methods, Discussion and Other Information sections. ConclusionsThis study demonstrates the potential of LLMs to automate reporting quality assessment in MR studies. Our results suggest that reporting quality still needs to be improved, and further efforts are required to promote the use of STROBE-MR. Our findings also suggest potential refinements to the STROBE-MR guideline to support more consistent application. 1 Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSCan large language models (LLMs) accurately assess adherence to the STROBE-MR reporting guideline in Mendelian randomization (MR) studies, and what patterns can we observe in MR reporting? FindingsThe LLM-based approach achieved good agreement with human consensus (89.0%) and identified substantial variation in reporting quality across STROBE-MR items and sections. No improvement in number of items reported was observed since the introduction of the STROBE-MR guideline. MeaningLLMs can enable scalable assessment of reporting guideline compliance, providing a practical approach for monitoring reporting quality. Further efforts are needed to promote the use of reporting guidelines for MR studies.

papers.title: Effects of a clinic-based reproductive empowerment intervention on reproductive coercion, intimate partner violence, and pregnancy outcomes: A cluster-controlled trial in Nairobi Kenya
papers.abstract: BackgroundTo address reproductive coercion and intimate partner violence, the ARCHES (Addressing Reproductive Coercion in Health Settings) intervention was adapted for clinics in Nairobi, Kenya and evaluated to assess impacts on reproductive coercion (primary outcome), physical and sexual intimate partner violence (primary outcomes) and incident pregnancy (secondary outcome). MethodsA parallel, non-blinded, non-randomized, cluster-controlled trial in six health clinics (1:1 allocation) was conducted. Clinics were allocated to receive ARCHES provider training or no additional training based on feasibility. Non-pregnant, non-sterilized female clients seeking family planning services were recruited. Inverse probability by treatment weighting (IPTW) used in difference-in-differences modified intent-to-treat (mITT) and as-treated approaches to assess the change in primary outcomes. ResultsA total of 659 women were recruited (328 ARCHES, 331 control). ARCHES was associated with significantly greater reductions in physical intimate partner violence compared to controls [mITT beta -0.98 (-1.58, -0.39), as-treated beta -0.56 (-1.19. 0.07)]. Both groups experienced reductions in reproductive coercion and sexual intimate partner violence decreased in both groups but controls showed greater reductions in reproductive coercion, and differences in sexual violence were not significant in as-treated models. ARCHES participants had lower odds of incident pregnancy at six-month follow-up [mITT AOR 0.42 (0.27, 0.67), as-treated AOR 0.29 (0.08. 1.02)]. ConclusionsARCHES may improve womens safety and reproductive agency in Nairobi. Further study is required to clarify effects on reproductive coercion and sexual intimate partner violence. Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov [NCT03534401]

papers.title: Anopheles Mosquito Distribution and Malaria Outbreak Risk Assessment in Georgia, USA (2001 2025): Implications for Surveillance and Preparedness.
papers.abstract: Competent malaria vector species in Georgia represents an emerging public health threat. Despite the successful elimination of endemic malaria transmission from the United States, the entomological conditions necessary for re-establishment of local transmission still persists across ecologically permissive regions of the south-eastern United States. However, no comprehensive, county-level assessment of Anopheles mosquito distribution and associated malaria outbreak risk has been conducted across the state. This study analyzed 2,716 Anopheles collection records, representing 11,265 individual specimens, from 24 years of surveillance data (2001-2025). Results classified Fulton County as a high risk hot spot and critical convergence zone for malaria outbreak with the most significantly highest risk score (25), Anopheles population density (2,561) and elevated MIR activity (> 4.1%). Glynn and Lowndes counties were designated as moderate risk (15 and 12 respectively), driven primarily by substantial Anopheles populations. Conversely, DeKalb County, despite exhibiting the highest individual infection rate (MIR: 6.67%), was classified low risk (Score: 10) due to lower Anopheles abundance. Our results underscore the need for improved mosquito surveillance in high-risk counties, to address the dual health threat of arboviral and potential human malaria outbreaks under current climate change scenarios in Georgia.

papers.title: Rapid Neurotoxicity of Transfluthrin Volatiles and Spatial Repellency of Alternate Deterrents Against Host Seeking Black Flies, Simulium Vittatum (Diptera: Simuliidae).
papers.abstract: Spatial repellants are novel tools that aim to disrupt host seeking behavior in hematophagous insects. Outdoor spatial repellents succeed only when the aerodynamic channel is predictable enough to maintain a behavioral repellent field. Though standardized bioassays are essential for characterizing deterrent mediated behavioral responses, substantial knowledge gaps remain about the practical use of high throughput assays to evaluate repellency in outdoor biting species such as Simulium species. This is particularly relevant within the context of spatial repellent formulations for outdoor use. This study evaluated the comparative spatial repellency, knockdown and lethality thresholds of transfluthrin, permethrin, DEET (N, N diethyl meta toluamide), citronella oil and neem oil against host-seeking adult black flies (Diptera: Simuliidae). Concentration response data obtained (T=15, 30mins,1hr and 24hrs) across different concentration scales (0.001ug-10mg/cm2) were analyzed using a nonlinear regression to four parameter logistic equations to calculate half repellency (EC50), half knockdown (KC50) and half lethality (L50) concentration thresholds respectively. Results revealed that black flies exhibited significant repellency, knock down and lethality rates towards transfluthrin in horizontal orientation compared to DEET, permethrin, citronella and neem oil ({chi}{superscript 2} = 48.99, df = 32, P = 0.028). Driven by rapid vapor phase, transfluthrin demonstrated unparalleled repellency at a concentration of 0.1ug/cm2 in horizontal orientation (EC50 values = 0.0201 g/cm{superscript 2}) and vertical orientation (EC50 values = 0.030 g/cm{superscript 2}) compared to DEET (1h EC50 = 39.72 g/cm{superscript 2}). 1h KC50 values revealed rapid knockdown effects (0.0259 g/cm{superscript 2}) compared to DEET (38.24 g/cm{superscript 2}) evidenced by rapid progression of neurotoxic hyper excitation in black flies in both orientations. Permethrin showed least repellency nor knockdown rates even at the highest concentrations (10mg/cm2). Compound concentration significantly impacted chemical diffusion dynamics ({chi}{superscript 2} = 75.85, df = 36, P = 0.000116), revealing that total compound loss through time depends heavily on chemical type. In conclusion, results from this study validates dose dependent spatial repellency of transfluthrin against the outdoor biting insect vector, Simulium vittatum in varied orientation placements using a high throughput repellency assay. This underscores the potential of spatial repellent compounds as a promising novel tool against both vectors of onchocerciasis, Simulium damnosum s.l. and vesicular stomatitis virus, Simulium vittatum.

papers.title: Data collection and analysis toolkit for maternal and neonatal health research and surveillance during epidemic threats: a pilot testing and mixed-methods evaluation
papers.abstract: Standardized outcome reporting is essential to generate timely and comparable evidence during epidemics. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed the Maternal and Neonatal Health during Epidemic Threats Core Outcome Set (MNH-EPI-COS) and a complementary Data Collection and Analysis Toolkit to support its implementation. Before global dissemination, the Toolkit required pilot testing to assess its usability, acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility across diverse research settings, identify challenges encountered by end users, and inform required improvements and refinements to the Toolkit. A four-phased mixed-methods evaluation was conducted with five research teams from Brazil, Honduras, India, Rwanda, and the United Kingdom. Teams received training and piloted all Toolkit components using retrospective datasets from previous epidemic contexts. Evaluation methods included structured feedback forms, observation of check-in meetings, and a virtual consultation. Findings informed an iterative process of refinement of the Toolkit components. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. Twenty participants with expertise in epidemiology, clinical research, REDCap administration, and data and management analysis completed the pilot. The REDCap project, R scripts, and supporting materials (reference guide, virtual training session, and videos) were consistently rated as clear, well-structured, and feasible to use. Paper-based case report forms (CRFs) were comprehensive but required refinement, particularly regarding redundancy, and alignment with electronic forms. Teams emphasized the need for multilingual materials, specialized training in R, and strengthened data quality controls to enhance the quality of the evidence generated. The WHO MNH-EPI-COS Data Collection and Analysis Toolkit demonstrated strong usability, acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility across diverse settings. The findings informed targeted refinements and support the Toolkits readiness for broader implementation to strengthen maternal and neonatal health research and surveillance during epidemics. Future evaluations should include prospective, real-time data collection during active outbreaks to further assess and strengthen the Toolkits performance under operational epidemic conditions.

papers.title: Current tobacco use and associated factors among school-going adolescents in the Republic of Congo: Secondary analysis of the 2019 Global Youth Tobacco Survey and development of a simple identification score
papers.abstract: Data on adolescent tobacco use in the Republic of Congo are scarce, despite a 2012 tobacco control law and 2018 decrees banning smoking in public places and tobacco advertising, promotion and sponsorship. This study aimed to estimate current tobacco product use among Congolese middle school students, identify associated factors, and develop a simple score to identify current use. Secondary analysis of the cross-sectional 2019 Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS). Current use was defined as self-reported use, in the past 30 days, of cigarettes (CR7), other smoked tobacco products (CR10) or smokeless tobacco (CR14). The estimates and regression models accounted for the sampling weights, 34 strata and 70 primary sampling units. A point-based score was developed from eight questionnaire-based factors and evaluated via cross-validation, which was grouped by primary sampling unit. Among the 6,297 students with a usable tobacco use status, 842 reported current use; the weighted prevalence was 13.5% (95% CI: 11.1-16.3%). The full model included 5,251 students, 597 of whom were current users. Being offered free tobacco by a tobacco company representative (aOR = 3.05), exposure to smoke at home (aOR = 2.71), seeing teachers smoke at school (aOR = 2.60) and exposure to smoke in enclosed public places (aOR = 2.02) were associated with current use. The score, ranging from 0 to 18 points, had a weighted AUROC of 0.771 in the development data and 0.765 in the grouped cross-validation data. Current tobacco use affects a substantial proportion of middle-school students. The associations with social and commercial exposures support the strengthening of prevention and the enforcement of existing legislation. The score is exploratory and requires external validation before any operational use.

papers.title: Examining the Influence of Displaced Populations on Tuberculosis Transmission: A Benue State Case Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundTuberculosis (TB) remains a significant public health challenge, particularly among displaced populations. These environments foster TB transmission due to overcrowding, poor living conditions, and inadequate healthcare access ObjectivesTo compare the proportion of tuberculosis (TB) cases detected through screening among displaced populations residing in internally displaced persons (IDP) and refugee settings with that among the general population in Benue State, Nigeria. DesignQuantitative observational study comparing TB screening and diagnostic findings across displaced and general populations. SettingIDP camps, refugee settings and general-community screening locations in Benue State, Nigeria. ParticipantsA total of 1,938 individuals were screened: 1,143 in displaced settings and 795 in the general population. Participants were assessed for presumptive TB and underwent the applicable diagnostic evaluation. Primary and secondary outcome measuresThe primary outcome was the proportion of screened individuals diagnosed with TB in displaced settings compared with the general population. Secondary outcomes were the numbers of presumptive TB cases and TB diagnoses classified as bacteriologically confirmed. ResultsAmong the 1,143 individuals screened in displaced settings, 128 presumptive TB cases were identified, with 46 confirmed cases (26 bacteriologically and 20 clinically). In contrast, only 3 TB cases (2 bacteriologically and 1 clinically) were detected among 795 individuals in the general population. The TB prevalence rate in displaced populations was 4.0%, significantly higher than the 0.4% observed in the general population. ConclusionsThe study confirms a heightened TB burden in displaced communities, emphasizing the need for enhanced screening, diagnosis, and treatment strategies.
